messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 53-year-old social worker, walked into the clinic with a posture that spoke of constant vigilance, his eyes scanning the waiting room before settling uneasily. His life had been irrevocably altered two years prior when, leaving a late client meeting in an unfamiliar part of town, he was cornered and sexually assaulted in a narrow, poorly lit alleyway. The assailant vanished into the night, leaving Mark with not just physical wounds, but an invisible scar that had reshaped his entire world.

From that night onward, the memory of the event became a relentless torment. When Mark tried to piece together what happened, the recall brought back the same terror he felt at the time, a visceral re-experiencing that left him breathless and shaking. An overwhelming sense of shame on recall also consumed him, making him feel profoundly tainted and isolated, even from his wife. Despite knowing what happened, he often felt unable to find words to describe it, as if the horror was too immense for language. The intense shame and terror that flooded Mark whenever he tried to revisit those moments made him desperate to push these thoughts out of his mind; he would try to suppress them, but they always returned, unbidden and unwelcome. This vivid, terrifying recollection instantly put him on high alert, convinced that danger was always lurking just beyond his periphery.

His constant vigilance, the gnawing certainty that something bad was about to happen, drove Mark to drastically change his routines. He began to avoid enclosed or confined spaces, preferring the stairs at his social work office building to the elevator, or arranging client meetings in more open, spacious rooms. He also found himself frequently looking behind him to check if someone was following him, especially when walking to his car after work, a habit that grew out of an unshakeable feeling that he was being watched. He avoided going to unfamiliar places, turning down invitations to new restaurants or social gatherings, because he felt he couldn't adequately assess the danger there. Ironically, this pervasive sense of threat only served to make the memory of his assault feel more immediate and real, as if it could happen again at any moment. The fear he felt in his daily life would summon the terror of that night, making the past feel like a constant, looming present.

While these avoidance tactics offered fleeting relief, they ultimately reinforced his belief that the world was a dangerous place, making him even more certain that something bad was happening whenever there was a delay, like a late bus or a client running behind schedule. He found himself consumed by rumination about how to get even with his assailant, replaying scenarios in his mind, which offered no peace and only deepened his sense of agitation and unresolved anger. This constant internal battle made him irritable and distant, straining his marriage as his wife struggled to understand his withdrawal. His capacity for empathy, once a cornerstone of his social work practice, suffered as his own internal turmoil and hypervigilance overshadowed his ability to connect with clients.

Mark’s wife eventually insisted he seek help, noticing how much he had changed and how his fear had begun to define their lives. He came to therapy exhausted, trapped in a relentless cycle of fear and avoidance, deeply ashamed of his struggles, but desperate for a way to escape the tightening grip of his past.
